Chiggers, also known as berry bugs or harvest mites, are tiny parasitic arachnids that are members of the Trombiculidae family. They are found throughout the world but are most common in forests, grassy fields, gardens, parks, and in wild berry patches where their preferred hosts live. They're particularly prevalent in summer and early fall. 

Chiggers start their life cycle as eggs, then grow into nymphs, before becoming adults. Only the larvae bite humans and feed on our skin. Chiggers can't burrow into the skin, but they attach themselves to their host and inject enzymes that destroy tissue. They then feed on the dead tissue. 

The bites can cause intense itching and small red bumps, usually where the skin is thin or where clothing is tight. Itching usually occurs several hours after the chiggers attach to the skin. The itching is not caused by the chigger biting the skin, but by the body's reaction to the digestive enzymes.

Chigger bites are not dangerous, but they can be very uncomfortable. Over-the-counter treatments can help with the itching, but the best way to prevent chigger bites is to avoid walking in tall grass and other areas where chiggers may be present, and to use bug spray when you're in chigger territory.
  
Contrary to popular belief, chiggers do not actually stay on a person's body after a bite. They fall off once they are done feeding. Therefore, treatments that claim to "suffocate" chiggers are typically ineffective, because the chigger is no longer present. While certain diseases in Asia are transmitted via chiggers, in the United States, chiggers are not known to transmit disease.
